n: The covenant from chapter 9 is now sealed. Nehemiah, the governor, signs first, leading by example. Zidkijah may have been his secretary or a high official.

f.g: Pressed their personal seal (a signet) onto the document as a binding signature.

n: The priests’ names begin. Many of these seem to be names of priestly families or divisions, signed by their current heads, as the similar list in Nehemiah 12 suggests.

f.g: A priestly family name here, not the prophet.

n: Pashur’s family had several members who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:22); now its head pledges loyalty to the covenant.
Hattush may be the descendant of David who came with Ezra, or a priest of the same name.
Meremoth, who helped rebuild two sections of the wall, now helps seal the covenant. Physical and spiritual rebuilding go together.
A Daniel and a Baruch sign — names shared with famous figures, though these are different men.
Abijah was the name of an ancient priestly division; John the Baptist’s father Zacharias belonged to it centuries later.
The list of 21 priests ends. Taken together, the priestly families of Judah publicly bind themselves to God’s law.
The Levites sign next. Jeshua and Kadmiel were Levite family names going back to the first return.
Several of these Levites had helped explain the law to the people when Ezra read it (Nehemiah 8:7).
More Levites add their seals.
Sherebiah, the wise Levite who came with Ezra, also signs.
The seventeen Levite signers end with Hodijah, Bani, and Beninu.
Now the lay leaders. Many signatures are family names from the list of returnees (Nehemiah 7), signed by each clan’s head.
Azgad and Bebai were large clans in the returnee lists.
Adonijah may be the same family as Adonikam in the earlier lists. Bigvai and Adin were also leading clans.

f.g: Possibly the same family called Adonikam in Nehemiah 7:18.

n: Ater and Hizkijah together recall the family “Ater of Hezekiah” (Nehemiah 7:21).

f.g: Another form of the name Hezekiah.

n: Hashum and Bezai, family names from the returnee register.
Anathoth, a town name, appears here as a signer — perhaps the leader representing that town.
Meshullam was a common name; Hezir also names an old priestly division, though here it is among the laymen.
Meshezabeel and Zadok also appear among the wall builders, showing many signers had worked with their own hands on the wall.

f.g: A name later borne by a high priest (Nehemiah 12:11).

n: Pelatiah, Hanan, and Anaiah add their seals. Anaiah had stood beside Ezra when the law was read.
Hoshea shares the original name of Joshua; Hashub had also built a section of the wall.
Hallohesh was the father of Shallum, who repaired the wall with his daughters (Nehemiah 3:12).
Rehum and others sign. These names, mostly unknown to us, were people who made a public commitment to God.
Ahijah, Hanan, and Anan sign.
The list ends with Baanah, perhaps a descendant of the leader of that name from the first return. In all, about 84 leaders sealed the covenant.
Everyone else joins too — temple workers, families, wives, sons, and daughters — anyone old enough to understand. The covenant was for the whole community, not just leaders.

f.w: every one having knowledge, and having understanding
f.g: All who were old enough to understand what they were promising.

f.w: separated themselves from the people of the lands

n: They join their leaders in a solemn oath, calling a curse upon themselves if they break it. They promise to keep the whole law of Moses.

f.w: entered into a curse, and into an oath
f.g: Swore an oath and accepted penalties for breaking it.

n: First specific promise: no marriages outside the covenant. This was the problem Ezra had faced (Ezra 9–10).

f.w: we would not give our daughters unto the people of the land

n: Second: no buying or selling on the Sabbath or holy days. Third: let the land rest every seventh year and cancel debts then, as the law required.
Fourth: each person will give a yearly temple tax of a third of a shekel. Willingly taxing themselves showed real commitment to God’s house.

f.w: the third part of a shekel

n: The money pays for the bread of the presence, the daily offerings, Sabbath and feast offerings, and sin offerings that made atonement for Israel — all pointing toward Christ’s great Atonement.

f.g: The “bread of the presence,” twelve loaves kept before the Lord in the temple (Leviticus 24:5-9).
The daily grain offering; “meat” means food.

f.w: to make an atonement for Israel

n: They cast lots to schedule which families would bring firewood for the altar, whose fire was never to go out.
They will bring the first harvest of fields and trees each year to the temple — giving God the first and best, not the leftovers.
Firstborn sons were redeemed by a payment, and firstborn animals were brought to the priests, as the law of Moses required.
They promise to bring offerings of bread dough, fruit, wine, and oil to the priests, and a tithe — a tenth — of their crops to the Levites in their towns.

f.w: tithes of our ground unto the Levites

f.g: The farming towns where crops were grown.

n: A priest would supervise when the Levites collected tithes, and the Levites would in turn give a tenth of what they received to the temple storehouse.
The covenant ends with a summary vow: “We will not forsake the house of our God.” Supporting the temple was a sign of loyalty to God Himself. Chapter 13 shows how hard this promise was to keep.

f.w: we will not forsake the house of our God
